question: Before anyone refines it, where does sugar come from — and what did people sweeten their food with in the meantime?
summary: For most of this folio there is no sugar in the sense that later folios mean: no crystals, no trade, no recipes. There is a plant — a tall grass from the New Guinea lowlands whose pith was chewed — and there are the sweeteners that every other farming people actually used: honey and dates. Sugarcane begins as a chewing cane, a local crop of one region, and the folio follows it from the wild canes to the first signs of the cultivated plant ([[w1]], [[te1]]).

The picture is built from two very different kinds of evidence. The sweeteners of the Near East and Europe are documented by pictures, pot residues and plant remains ([[e2]], [[ec2]], [[ec3]]); sugarcane itself is documented mainly by genomes and by reconstructed words ([[te1]], [[th1]]), with a single archaeological find ([[ec4]]). The result is a story about origins that is secure in outline and thin in detail: cane was domesticated in New Guinea and its neighbourhood, and it travelled with seafaring peoples across the Pacific long before it reached any continent's kitchens ([[x2]]).
What to take from the folio: sugar is not an ancient commodity but an ancient *plant*. The industry, the trade and the politics all come later; this folio is the ground they stand on.

themes.title: The plant: a New Guinea domestication
text: Two wild canes frame everything: *Saccharum robustum*, the sweet-pith ancestor of New Guinea and the islands east of the Wallace line, and *S. spontaneum*, a hardy grass of the continental belt that will later supply the hybrids. The genomic work places domestication at roughly 8,000 years ago, in a landscape where people were already cultivating wetland plots at Kuk.

themes.title: How the cane moved: old model, new model
text: The older botanical account (three diffusions from New Guinea, beginning in the eighth millennium BC) was the standard story for decades; the 2025 genomic study ties the continental-Asian diversification to human movements only about 3,000 years ago, and the island Pacific to voyagers from about 1500 BC. Treat the early dates of the old model as contested, and the voyager route as the better-supported one.

themes.title: Sweetness without sugar: honey and dates
text: Honey is the sweetener of the early Near East and Europe, and the evidence for it is older and firmer than anything for cane: managed hives in an Egyptian sun temple, beeswax in Neolithic cooking pots, a northern limit for the honeybee. Dates play the same role in the Gulf and Mesopotamia. Sugar will eventually displace both, which is what makes this the right place to start.

turning_points.text: Sugarcane is domesticated from wild robustum cane in New Guinea and nearby islands.
Beeswax in Turkish cooking pots shows farmers already exploiting the honeybee — the sweetener that sugar will replace.
A word for sugarcane can be reconstructed for Proto-Austronesian: the crop already had a name among the seafaring peoples.
The first sugarcane in the archaeological record, from New Guinea.
A relief in Niuserre's sun temple shows the first known beekeeper, honey as a managed, stored product.
Voyagers carry cane through the Melanesian and Polynesian islands, where it hybridises with a second, unknown ancestor.

how_to_read: Start with *Technology* and *World* for the plant, then *Exchange* for how it moved. The *Economy* and *Expression* lanes carry the honey-and-dates side of the story, which is the real sweetening of this period.

Several lanes (Power, Conflict, Order, Belief, Lives) are empty by design: nothing in the sources lets us say who ruled or fought over cane before the next folio. The Nexus shows how the few strands connect. The next folio picks up when cane reaches the mainland of Asia.

sources.intro: Prehistory leaves no accounts, so the folio leans on three kinds of secondary evidence: genomic and botanical studies, linguistic reconstruction, and archaeology of sweeteners other than cane. Almost nothing here rests on a text the folio's author read in the original.
main: The 2025 *Cell* genomic study of wild and cultivated *Saccharum*, read through its abstract and the CIRAD press release, carries the domestication and Pacific-dispersal entries ([[te1]], [[x2]]).
Needham's *Science and Civilisation in China* 6.3 (Daniels and Menzies), the Daniels sugarcane chapters and Kieschnick supply the older botanical and archaeological frame ([[ec4]], [[w1]]).
Denham, Golson and Hughes on Kuk Swamp is the one chapter-level source, for the New Guinea agricultural setting ([[ec1]]).
contested: The age of the Bicorp honey-gatherer painting is disputed, and recent work questions even the climber's sex ([[e1]]).
Brandes's three diffusions are an older model that the genomic work now contradicts in its dating ([[x1]]).
The Proto-Austronesian cane word is cited from summaries; the cognate set itself was not checked ([[th1]]).
gaps: The *Cell* paper itself was not retrieved; the genomic claims rest on its abstract and a press release.
No direct archaeobotanical evidence for cane in the Pacific or New Guinea beyond the single c.2500 BC find ([[ec4]]); more would sharpen the domestication date.
The honey and date entries are context drawn from secondary summaries and from other folios; a specialist history of Near Eastern sweeteners would deepen them.
